title: Bankruptcy disclosure: Sanctions remain discretionary enforcement
desc: Organizes proof-of-claim documentation duties before remedies, distinguishing disclosure enforcement and technical reference corrections from AI-generated evidence.

kps.k: The supplied material concerns bankruptcy disclosure and enforcement, not machine-generated evidence.
kps.d: Despite the source label naming proposed Evidence Rule 707, the excerpts address Bankruptcy Rules 3001 and 2007.1. They document proposed corrections and disclosure requirements, rather than arguments about AI evidence. They contain no substantive disagreement or evidence about machine-generated evidence, so they cannot support conclusions on that debate.

kps.k: The committee seeks to restore sanctions coverage while organising Rule 3001 around disclosure duties followed by enforcement.
kps.d: The proposal moves revolving consumer-credit disclosures to subdivision (c)(3) and sanctions to (c)(4). It also replaces the sanctions cross-reference to specified paragraphs with a reference to all of subdivision (c). The committee distinguishes the organisational change from the correction of an inadvertent substantive restriction introduced by the restyled rule effective December 1, 2024. The practical implication is restored enforcement coverage, not a new policy governing AI.

kps.k: Rule 3001 links proof-of-claim filing to supporting documents and account-specific disclosures.
kps.d: The supplied text requires creditors to file underlying writings, subject to the consumer-credit exception, or explain their loss or destruction. Individual-debtor cases require additional financial disclosures, including itemised principal and prepetition charges, applicable default-cure amounts, and residential-security documentation. Open-end or revolving consumer-credit claims generally require account ownership and transaction-history information, except when secured by the debtor’s real property. Creditors must send the underlying writing within 30 days after a party in interest sends a written request. These provisions give parties concrete documentation requirements and a route to obtain supporting records.

kps.k: Disclosure failures expose claim holders to discretionary remedies, not automatic penalties.
kps.d: In individual-debtor cases, courts may act after notice and a hearing. They may exclude undisclosed information from contested matters or adversary proceedings unless the failure was substantially justified or harmless. They may also award appropriate relief, including reasonable expenses and attorney’s fees caused by the failure. The text therefore pairs disclosure enforcement with procedural safeguards and limits on evidentiary exclusion; it does not establish how frequently courts impose these remedies.

kps.k: Rule 2007.1 corrections repair appointment-disclosure references rather than establish a new disclosure regime.
kps.d: The supplied provisions require identification of an appointee, disclosure of relevant connections and consulted parties, and the appointee’s verified connections statement. The committee replaces references to nonexistent numbered clauses with the correct subparagraph reference because the relevant entities appear in bullet points. The practical change clarifies which entities the disclosures cover.

vlens.an: The supplied regulators, courts and professional-bodies source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition. It treats the Rule 3001 changes as both an organisational revision—placing sanctions after the disclosure duties they enforce—and a correction restoring coverage inadvertently narrowed in the 2024 restyling. It also confirms that enforcement is discretionary and procedurally constrained: a court may impose remedies only after notice and a hearing, with evidentiary exclusion limited where nondisclosure was substantially justified or harmless. The source additionally supports the synthesis’s boundary-setting conclusion that the excerpts concern bankruptcy disclosure rules and technical references, notwithstanding the machine-generated-evidence wording in the source label. There is no material internal disagreement: the only variation is between technical reorganisation, substantive restoration of sanctions coverage, and correction of erroneous cross-references. Because this facet contains one curated source, its position should not be treated as representative of regulators, courts or professional bodies generally.

elens.an: The supplied 2025 source supports the cluster’s principal proposition. It distinguishes the organisation of Rule 3001—placing sanctions after the disclosure duties they enforce—from a substantive correction restoring sanctions coverage inadvertently narrowed by the 2024 restyling. It also confirms that enforcement remains discretionary: after notice and a hearing, a court may exclude undisclosed information or award appropriate relief, subject to substantial-justification and harmlessness safeguards. Internal variation is therefore complementary rather than conflicting: some amendments are technical or organisational, while the cross-reference correction has a restorative substantive effect. The Rule 2007.1 material likewise corrects erroneous references rather than creating a new disclosure regime. Although the source title mentions machine-generated evidence, the supplied excerpts do not address that subject. Because this is a curated single-source record, it establishes this source’s alignment but not the prevalence of that view in 2025.
